contexts.title: Evaluating the Definite Integral of a Radical Function

canonical.:question/problem:
Calculate $$
\displaystyle\int_1^4\sqrt x\, \textrm d x.
$$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
Taking the antiderivative and evaluating the difference at the bounds, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{4}\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{4}{x}^{1/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3/2}{|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}({4}^{3/2}-{1}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}(\sqrt{64}-1) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}(8-1) \\  & =\frac{14}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

\displaystyle {\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x.
$$
nearby_complete.:question/worked-solution:
Taking the antiderivative and evaluating the difference at the bounds, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{4}{x}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-1/2+1}}{-\frac{1}{2}+1}{|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =2{x}^{1/2}{|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =2({4}^{1/2}-{1}^{1/2}) \\  & =2(\sqrt{4}-1) \\  & =2(2-1) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

contexts.title: Calculating the Curl of a Vector Field

canonical.:question/problem: Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F} = y\,\mathbf{i} + x^2\,\mathbf{j} - 2z\,\mathbf{k}.$ Evaluate $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F}$ at the point  $\left(-1,0,2\right).$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
If $\mathbf{F}=P\,\mathbf{i}+Q\,\mathbf{j}+R\,\mathbf{k}$ is a vector field on $\mathbb{R}^3$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $\mathbf F$ all exist, then the curl of $\mathbf F$ is the vector field given by

$$
\mathrm {curl}\, \mathbf F =\nabla\times\mathbf{F}=\left| {\begin{array}{ccc}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ {\displaystyle \frac{\partial }{\partial  x}} & {\displaystyle \frac{\partial }{\partial  y}} & {\displaystyle \frac{\partial }{\partial  z}} \\ P & Q & R\end{array}} \right|.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ y & {x}^{2} & -2z\end{vmatrix} \\  & =[\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2z)-\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2})]i-[\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2z)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(y)]j+[\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})-\frac{∂}{∂y}(y)]k \\  & =(0-0)i-(0-0)j+(2x-1)k \\  & =(2x-1)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\textrm {curl}\, \mathbf{F}$ at the point $\left(-1,0,2\right),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(\text{curl}\,F)(-1,0,2) & =(2(-1)-1)\,k=-3\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

nearby_complete.:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j+R\,k$ is a vector field on ${R}^{3}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the curl of $F$ is the vector field given by

$$
curl\,F=∇\times F=\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ P & Q & R\end{vmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ {z}^{2} & 2xy & x{y}^{2}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =[\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2})-\frac{∂}{∂z}(2xy)]i-[\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2})-\frac{∂}{∂z}({z}^{2})]j+[\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy)-\frac{∂}{∂y}({z}^{2})]k \\  & =(2xy-0)\,i-({y}^{2}-2z)\,j+(2y-0)\,k \\  & =2xy\,i-({y}^{2}-2z)\,j+2y\,k \\  & =⟨2xy,\,2z-{y}^{2},\,2y⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
curl\,F=∇\times F=\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ P & Q & R\end{vmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ {e}^{y+z} & 1 & xyz\end{vmatrix} \\  & =[\frac{∂}{∂y}(xyz)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(1)]i-[\frac{∂}{∂x}(xyz)-\frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{y+z})]j+[\frac{∂}{∂x}(1)-\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{y+z})]k \\  & =(xz-0)i-(yz-{e}^{y+z})j+(0-{e}^{y+z})k \\  & =xz\,i+({e}^{y+z}-yz)j-{e}^{y+z}\,k.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}(\text{curl}\,F)(2,1,-1) & =2(-1)\,i+({e}^{1+(-1)}-1(-1))j-{e}^{1+(-1)}\,k \\  & =-2\,i+2\,j-k.\end{aligned}
$$

contexts.title: Calculating an Area Using Green's Theorem

canonical.:question/problem:
Consider the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C=C_1 \cup C_2,$ where 

- $C_1$ is parametrized by $\mathbf{r}_1(t) =-2 t^4 \: \mathbf{i} + t^3 \: \mathbf{j}$ for $t \in \left[-1,1\right],$ and

- $C_2$ is parametrized by $\mathbf{r}_2(t) = -2\: \mathbf{i} -t \: \mathbf{j}$ for $t \in \left[-1,1\right].$

Use Green's theorem to find the area of the region.

![](images/14/147e8fdd97fc938ae5482b70d7215483956a860ee3ce69ae5bbebd111dcc343b.png)
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
First, let $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0.$

Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented, and  

$$
\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 0 - \left(-1\right) = 1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y) = -y$ and $Q(x,y) = 0,$ we get

$$
\oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}x + Q \: \text{d}y = -\oint\limits_C y \: \text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivatives of $\mathbf r_1(t)$ and $\mathbf r_2(t)$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}_{1}:\, & {r}_{1}^{′}(t)=-8{t}^{3}\,i+3{t}^{2}\,j \\ {C}_{2}:\, & {r}_{2}^{′}(t)=-j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}-{∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x & =-{∮}_{{C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}}y\,dx \\  & =-{∮}_{{C}_{1}}y\,dx-{∮}_{{C}_{2}}y\,dx \\  & =-{\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{3}\cdot (-8{t}^{3})\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{-1}^{1}(-t)\cdot 0\,\text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{6}\,\text{d}t+0 \\  & =8[\frac{{t}^{7}}{7}]_{-1}^{1} \\  & =8\cdot \frac{2}{7} \\  & =\frac{16}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

- ${C}_{2}$ is parametrized by ${r}_{2}(t)=2\,i+t\,j$ for $t\in [-1,1].$

Use Green's theorem to find the area of the region.
nearby_complete.:question/worked-solution:
First, let $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0.$

Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0-(-1)=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y=-{∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivatives of ${r}_{1}(t)$ and ${r}_{2}(t)$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}_{1}:\, & {r}_{1}^{′}(t)=4t\,i-3{t}^{2}\,j \\ {C}_{2}:\, & {r}_{2}^{′}(t)=j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}-{∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x & =-{∮}_{{C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}}y\,dx \\  & =-{∮}_{{C}_{1}}y\,dx-{∮}_{{C}_{2}}y\,dx \\  & =-{\int }_{-1}^{1}(-{t}^{3})\cdot 4t\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{-1}^{1}t\cdot 0\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{4}\,\text{d}t-0 \\  & =4[\frac{{t}^{5}}{5}]_{-1}^{1} \\  & =4\cdot \frac{2}{5} \\  & =\frac{8}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/2a/2a89a14bced6f6700614cfad216070154cae165785458f817ea06d266edfde4e.png)

Use Green's theorem to find the area of the region enclosed by the curve 
$C$ parametrized as $r(t)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,i-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ 
for $t\in [0,\pi ].$
nearby_complete.:question/worked-solution:
First, let $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x.$

Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is negatively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1-0=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & =-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Notice that we have to take the line integral with a minus sign since our path is negatively oriented. 

Substituting $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we get

$$
-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y=-{∮}_{C}x\,\text{d}y.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,i-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate our line integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{∮}_{C}x\,dy & =-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\cdot (-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\pi }2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-8{\int }_{1}^{-1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =8{\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{8}{3}{u}^{3}{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}({1}^{3}-(-1)^{3}) \\  & =\frac{16}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

$C$ parametrized as $r(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j$ 
for $t\in [\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{3\pi }{2}].$

Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented, and  

$$

$$

$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$

Finally, we can evaluate our line integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}x\,dy & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2{\int }_{1}^{-1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2{\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{u}^{3}{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}({1}^{3}-(-1)^{3}) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

contexts.title: Reducing the Line Integral of a Scalar Function Along a Curve to a Definite Integral

canonical.:question/problem:
Consider the line integral 

$$
\displaystyle \int \limits_{C} \dfrac{y^2}{x} \,\textrm ds,
$$

 where $C$ is the section of the curve $y = \dfrac{x^3}3$ between the points $(0,0)$ and $(3,9).$
Write the line integral in the form 

$$
\displaystyle\int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.
$$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $y=y(x).$ Therefore, by setting $x=t,$ we have $y = y(t) = \dfrac{t^3}{3}.$ This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle t, \dfrac{t^3}3 \right\rangle, \qquad 0 \le t \le 3,
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get the following:

$$

canonical.:question/problem:
Evaluate the integral $$
\displaystyle \int\limits_{C} \dfrac{y^3}{x^2} \, \text{d}s,
$$ where the curve $C$ is given by $y = x$ for $\, 0 \le x \le 4.$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $y=y(x).$ Therefore, by setting $x=t,$ we have $y = y(t) = t.$ This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle t, \: t \right\rangle, \qquad 0 \le t \le 4
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y) = \dfrac{y^3}{x^2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{{t}^{3}}{{t}^{2}}=t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{{y}^{3}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{4}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}t\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{4}t\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}{t}^{2}{|}_{0}^{4} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}({4}^{2}-{0}^{2}) \\  & =8\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
r(t)=⟨t,\,{e}^{t}⟩,\,0\le t\le \operatorname{ln}⁡3
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(u) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})j \\  & =i+{e}^{t}j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{({e}^{t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+{e}^{2t}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=2{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2({e}^{t})^{2}=2{e}^{2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}2{e}^{2t}\cdot \sqrt{1+{e}^{2t}}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}2{e}^{2t}\,\sqrt{1+{e}^{2t}}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

nearby_complete.:question/problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=2xy$ along the curve $y=\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}},$ $\,0\le x\le 2.$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(u) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{4-{t}^{2}})j \\  & =i-\frac{t}{\sqrt{4-{t}^{2}}}\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{\left(-\frac{t}{\sqrt{4-{t}^{2}}}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{{t}^{2}}{4-{t}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{4-{t}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=2xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2t\sqrt{4-{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
r(t)=⟨t,\,t⟩,\,0\le t\le 3
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(u) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =i+\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}

contexts.title: Converting an Integral Over an Annular Region to Polar Coordinates

canonical.:question/problem:
![](images/94/940f547f886f1b680cbb37ef950438e6a4f33bd3c84df28a5e00480631c97711.png)

The region $D$ in the first quadrant is enclosed between the quarter-circles of radii $3$ and $4,$ as shown above. What is
$$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_D \dfrac{1}{x^2+y^2} \: \textrm{d}A
$$
expressed in polar coordinates?
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

The region $D$ represents a portion of the washer enclosed between the circles of radii $3$ and $4$ centered at the origin. In polar coordinates $(r, \theta),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \Big\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 3 \leq r \leq 4, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2} \Big\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{1}{(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{3}^{4}\frac{r}{{r}^{2}({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{3}^{4}\frac{1}{r}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

canonical.:question/worked-solution:
Taking the antiderivative and evaluating the difference at the bounds, we get

contexts.title: Computing the Normal Line to a Parametric Curve

canonical.:question/problem:
![](images/9d/9dcc4c97bd296ef4627b02b6cfafcdb643f475cd8dacd36a820db760bd6fb045.png)

The following parametric equations define the curve shown above:

$$
x=2\cos{t} +\sin{2t},\quad y=\cos{t} - 2\sin{2t},\qquad 0\leq t<2\pi
$$

Calculate the equation of the normal to the curve at the point where $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ (shown as a dashed line in the plot above).
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) \\  & =\sqrt{2}+1, \\  \\ y & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-2(1) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-2.\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the normal at the point $\left(\sqrt{2}+1,\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} -2\right).$ For this, we need to find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x},$ which means we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
x'(t) = -2\sin t + 2\cos 2t, \qquad y'(t) = -\sin t - 4 \cos 2t .
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{-\operatorname{sin}⁡t-4\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t} \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t+4\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4},$ the slope $m$ of the tangent line is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=\pi /4} \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)+4\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)}{2(\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right))} \\  & =-\frac{\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2}+4(0)}{2(0-\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2})} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope $m_n$ of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of $m$:

$$
m_n = -\dfrac{1}{m} = -\dfrac{1}{\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)} = -2
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the normal line, we use the point-slope form 

$$
y - y_1 = m_n(x-x_1),
$$

with

$$
(x_1,y_1) = \left(\sqrt{2}+1,\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} -2\right), \qquad m_n=-2,
$$

and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-2) & =-2(x-(\sqrt{2}+1)) \\ y-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+2 & =-2x+2\sqrt{2}+2 \\ y+2x & =\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

contexts.title: Determining the Points Where the Tangent is Horizontal or Vertical

canonical.:question/problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations 

$$
x=t^2+3, \quad y=-t+1, \qquad -\infty <     t <    \infty.
$$

Determine the value of $t$ at which the tangent to the curve is vertical.
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
The slope $m$ of a tangent line to a curve defined parametrically is given by

$$
m = \dfrac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}.
$$

The tangent line is vertical if $x'(t)=0$ while $y'(t) \neq 0 .$

So, we first find the derivatives of $x$ and $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
x'(t) = 2t, \qquad y'(t) = -1 .
$$

Solving $x'(t) = 0$ gives

$$
2t=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad t=0.
$$

Note that $y'(0) = -1\neq 0.$ Therefore, we conclude that when $t = 0,$ the tangent to the curve is vertical.

$$

contexts.title: Computing the Tangent Line to a Parametric Curve

canonical.:question/problem:
Suppose that we have a curve defined by the parametric equations 

$$
x=2t+3, \quad y=t^3-4t, \qquad -\infty < t <\infty.
$$

What is the equation of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $t=-1?$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting $t=-1$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2(-1)+3=1, \\ y & =(-1)^{3}-4(-1)=-1+4=3.\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent line to the curve at the point $(1,3).$ The plot below shows the curve and the tangent line at this point.

![](images/0f/0fa3fc12e83e2a581499680145df9229917c7426e6a3d12c51d88e115a42033e.png)

To find the slope of the tangent line, we need to find $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
x'(t) = 2, \qquad y'(t) = 3t^2-4 .
$$

So, we have

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(t)}{x'(t)} = \dfrac{3t^2-4}{2}.
$$

At the point where $t=-1,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=-1} & =\frac{3(-1)^{2}-4}{2}=-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $(x_1,y_1) = (1,3)$ and the slope $m=-\dfrac{1}{2}.$ We get

$$
y - 3 = -\frac{1}{2}\left(x-1\right).
$$

\begin{aligned}y-0 & =\frac{\pi }{3}(x-2).\end{aligned}

$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent line to the curve at the point $(\frac{4}{3},1).$ 

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\left(\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\right) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(\frac{4}{3},1)$ and the slope $m=1.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-1 & =1\cdot (x-\frac{4}{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent crosses the $x$-axis when $y=0.$ At this point, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}0-1 & =1\cdot (x-\frac{4}{3}) \\ -1 & =x-\frac{4}{3} \\ x & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $(\frac{1}{3},\,0)$ is the $x$-intercept.

canonical.:question/problem: Let $\mathbf{a}=\langle 3,-4,1 \rangle$ and $\mathbf{b}=\langle -7,0,2 \rangle.$ Find $\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}.$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
Using the determinant formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}a\times b & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 3 & -4 & 1 \\ -7 & 0 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-4 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{vmatrix}i-\begin{vmatrix}3 & 1 \\ -7 & 2\end{vmatrix}j+\begin{vmatrix}3 & -4 \\ -7 & 0\end{vmatrix}k \\  & =((-4)\cdot 2-1\cdot 0)i-(3\cdot 2-1\cdot (-7))j+(3\cdot 0-(-4)\cdot (-7))k \\  & =-8i-13j-28k \\  & =⟨-8,-13,-28⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical.:question/problem: Simplify the expression $\sin x(2\cos x - \sin x) - \cos^2x.$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
First, we expand the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x-{cos}^{2}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we group the $\sin^2 x$ and $\cos^2 x$ terms. 

$$
2\sin x\cos x -(\sin^2x + \cos^2 x)
$$

Then, we use $\sin^2{x} + \cos^2{x} = 1$ to simplify the expression in the parentheses:

$$
2\sin x\cos x - 1
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\sin x(2\cos x - \sin x) - \cos^2x = 2\sin x\cos x - 1.
$$

canonical.:question/problem: Simplify the trigonometric expression $\dfrac{\sin{\theta}}{1+\cos{\theta}}+\cot{\theta}.$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rewrite the second term using the identity $\cot \theta = \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta},$ as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\sin{\theta}}{1+\cos{\theta}}+\dfrac{\cos{\theta}}{\sin{\theta}}
$$

Next, we put both terms over a common denominator, and combine the two fractions:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}+\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot (1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )} &= \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot (1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we simplify as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )} &= \frac{({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )} \\ &= \frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )} \\ &= \frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\ &= \operatorname{csc}⁡\theta\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\dfrac{\sin{\theta}}{1+\cos{\theta}}+\cot{\theta} = \csc\theta.
$$

$$

$$

$$

contexts.title: Finding the Divergence of a Vector Field in Two Dimensions

canonical.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}=\ln(2x+y)\,\mathbf{i}+ x^2e^{3y}\,\mathbf{j}.$ 
Evaluate $\nabla \cdot\mathbf{F}$ at the point $(1,0).$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
If $\mathbf{F}=P\,\mathbf{i}+Q\,\mathbf{j}$ is a vector field on $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $\mathbf F$ all exist, then the divergence of $\mathbf F$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}=\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F=\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot F & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y))+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}{e}^{3y}) \\  & =\frac{2}{2x+y}+3{x}^{2}{e}^{3y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf {F}$ at the point $(1,0),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(∇\cdot F)(1,0) & =\frac{2}{2(1)+0}+3(1)^{2}{e}^{3(0)} \\  & =1+3 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

nearby_complete.:question/problem: Given that $F=2x{y}^{2}\,i+4{x}^{2}y\,j,$ what is $\text{div}\,F?$

$$
\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot F & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x{y}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂y}(4{x}^{2}y) \\  & =2{y}^{2}+4{x}^{2} \\  & =4{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

If $V=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $V$ all exist, then the divergence of $V$ is given by

$$
∇\cdot V=\text{div}\,V=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,V & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy) \\  & =2xy+2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\text{div}\,V$ at the point $(1,1),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,V\,{|}_{(1,\,1)} & =2(1)(1)+2(1) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical.:question/problem: Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y) = e^{x+y} \, \mathbf{i} + 3xy \, \mathbf{j}.$ Evaluate the scalar curl of $\mathbf{F}$ at the point $(-1,1).$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf{i} + Q\,\mathbf{j}$ is a vector field on $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $\mathbf F$ all exist, then the *scalar* curl of $\mathbf{F}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3xy)-\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x+y}) \\  & =3y-{e}^{x+y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the scalar curl at the point $(-1,1),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})}_{(-1,1)} & =3(1)-{e}^{-1+1} \\  & =3-{e}^{0} \\  & =3-1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

nearby_complete.:question/problem: Consider the vector field $F(x,y)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)\,j.$ Evaluate the scalar curl of $F$ at the point $(\pi ,0).$
nearby_complete.:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the *scalar* curl of $F$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy))-\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡y) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\cdot y-x\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\  & =-y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)-x\operatorname{cos}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the scalar curl at the point $(\pi ,0),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})}_{(\pi ,0)} & =-0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi \cdot 0)-\pi \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(0) \\  & =0-\pi \cdot 1 \\  & =-\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

contexts.title: Applying Green's Theorem to Regions With Holes

canonical.:question/problem:
![](images/83/83bd636f3a294c641e171c5a8281aaa7068e1931a06229064314e8f96efd0c3a.png)

Calculate $$
\displaystyle\oint\limits_{\partial D} (x^2-3y)\, \mathrm{d}x + ( y^2+x)\,\mathrm{d}y,
$$ where $D$ is the annular region shown above.
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that
$$
\oint\limits_{C} P\,\mathrm{d}x + Q\,\mathrm{d}y 
= \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\textrm d A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)= x^2-3y$ and $Q(x,y)= y^2+x.$ So,

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = -3, \qquad 
\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} = 1.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{array}{cc}\underset{\partial  D}{∮} ( {x}^{2} - 3 y )  \mathrm{d} x + ( {y}^{2} + x )  \mathrm{d} y &  = \underset{D}{\iint } ( \frac{\partial  Q}{\partial  x} - \frac{\partial  P}{\partial  y} )  \text{d} A \\  &  = \underset{D}{\iint } ( 1 - ( - 3 ) )  \text{d} A \\  &  = \underset{D}{\iint } 4  \text{d} A \\  &  = 4 \underset{D}{\iint }  \text{d} A \\  &  = 4 \cdot  \text{Area} ( D ) \\  &  = 4 \cdot  ( \pi  \cdot  {4}^{2} - \pi  \cdot  {2}^{2} ) \\  &  = 4 \cdot  12 \pi  \\  &  = 48 \pi  .\end{array}
$$

contexts.title: Writing the Flux Across a Closed Surface as a Triple Integral

canonical.:question/problem: Let $S$ be the boundary of the finite solid region enclosed by the planes $x=-1,$ $x=1,$ $y=0,$ $y=1,$ and the surfaces $z=y$ and $z=1+x^2+y^2.$ Given that the surface $S$ is positively (outward) oriented and $\mathbf{F} = (x+z )\, \mathbf{i} + yz \, \mathbf{j} + x^2y \, \mathbf{k},$ express the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $S$ as a triple integral, and then as a repeated integral.
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
Let $R$ be a simple solid region bounded by a closed surface $S$ with positive (outward) orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $R,$ then the divergence theorem states that

$$
\iint\limits_{S} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{S}
= \iiint\limits_R \textrm{div}\,\mathbf{F} \: \textrm{d}V.
$$

Computing the divergence of $\mathbf{F},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+z)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(yz)+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}y) \\  & =1+z+0 \\  & =z+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the divergence theorem, we have

$$
\iint\limits_{S} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iiint\limits_R (z+1) \: \textrm{d}V,
$$

where $R$ is a type I solid region that can be written as

$$
R = \big\{ (x,y,z) \: : \:-1 \leq x \leq 1, \: 0 \leq y \leq 1, \: y \leq z \leq 1+x^2+y^2 \big\}.
$$

canonical.:question/problem: For which vector field is $f(x,y) = \sin(2x-y)$ a potential function?
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
A vector field $\mathbf F$ is conservative if it is the gradient of a scalar function $f.$ That is, there exists a function $f$ such that $\mathbf F = \nabla f.$ The function $f$ is called a potential function for $\mathbf F.$

To compute the vector field associated with a potential function $f,$ we compute its gradient:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-y))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-y))\,j \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x-y)\,i-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x-y)\,j \\  & =F\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector field that has $f$ as a potential function is

$$
\mathbf F = 2\cos(2x-y)\,\mathbf i -\cos(2x-y) \, \mathbf j.
$$

contexts.title: Finding a Parameter in a Given Conservative Vector Field

canonical.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field $$
\displaystyle \mathbf F = \dfrac{2ay}{1+9x^2} \, \mathbf i + \arctan{3x} \, \mathbf j
$$ on $\mathbb R^2$, where $a$ is a constant. Given that $\mathbf F$ is conservative, find the value of $a.$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
Let $\mathbf F(x,y) = P(x,y)\,\mathbf i+ Q(x,y)\,\mathbf j$ be a vector field with domain $D = \mathbb R^2,$ where $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives everywhere on $D.$ Then, we have the following theorem:

$\mathbf F$ *is conservative if and only if $$
\displaystyle \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x}
$$ everywhere on $D.$*

For the vector field $\mathbf F,$ the domain $D = \mathbb R^2,$ and we have

$$
P = \dfrac{2ay}{1+9x^2}, \qquad Q = \arctan{3x}.
$$

 
Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = \dfrac{2a}{1 + 9x^2}, 
\qquad 
\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} = \dfrac{3}{1 + 9x^2}.
$$

It's clear that the partial derivatives exist and are continuous on $\mathbb R^2.$ Equating the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2a}{1+9{x}^{2}} & =\frac{3}{1+9{x}^{2}} \\ 2a & =3 \\ a & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $a = \dfrac{3}{2}.$

nearby_complete.:question/problem: Consider the vector field $F=2ay\,i+(3-x)\,j$ on ${R}^{2}$, where $a$ is a constant. Given that $F$ is conservative, find the value of $a.$
nearby_complete.:question/worked-solution:
Let $F(x,y)=P(x,y)\,i+Q(x,y)\,j$ be a vector field with domain $D={R}^{2},$ where $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives everywhere on $D.$ Then, we have the following theorem:

$F$ *is conservative if and only if $\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}$ everywhere on $D.$*

For the vector field $F,$ the domain $D={R}^{2},$ and we have 

$$
P=2ay,\,Q=3-x.
$$

 

Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2a,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=-1.
$$

It's clear that the partial derivatives exist and are continuous on ${R}^{2}.$ Equating the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2a & =-1 \\ a & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $a=-\frac{1}{2}.$

Let $F(x,y)=P(x,y)\,i+Q(x,y)\,j$ be a vector field with domain $D={R}^{2},$ where $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives everywhere on $D.$ Then, we have the following theorem:

>$F$ *is conservative if and only if $\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}$ everywhere on $D.$*

For our vector field $F,$ the domain is $D={R}^{2},$ and we have 

$$
P=a{y}^{3}-1,\,Q=3x{y}^{2}+1.
$$

 

Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=3a{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=3{y}^{2}.
$$

It's clear that the partial derivatives exist and are continuous on ${R}^{2}.$ Equating the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3a{y}^{2} & =3{y}^{2} \\ 3a & =3 \\ a & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $a=1.$

For the vector field $F,$ we have $P=ay-2x{y}^{3}$ and $Q=x-3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$

contexts.title: Finding the Equation of a Level Curve

canonical.:question/problem: Find the equation of the level curve that passes through the point $G\big(\sqrt{5}, 1\big)$ for the function $f(x,y) = \dfrac{12y}{x^2-y^2}.$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the value of the function at $G$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
  f\big(\sqrt{5}, 1\big)&= \dfrac{12(1)}{\big(\sqrt{5}\big)^2 - 1^2} = 3\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the level curve that passes through $G\big(\sqrt{5}, 1\big)$ is the $3$-level curve.

Recall that the level curves for the function $f(x,y)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y) = c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=3.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =c \\ \frac{12y}{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} & =3 \\ 4y & ={x}^{2}-{y}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-4y-4 & =-4 \\ {x}^{2}-({y}^{2}+4y+4) & =-4 \\ {x}^{2}-(y+2)^{2} & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level curve that passes through $G\big(\sqrt{5}, 1\big)$ is the hyperbola $x^2 - (y+2)^2 = -4.$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,1) & =1(1)-2 \\  & =1-2 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the level curve that passes through $P(1,1)$ is the $-1$-level curve.

Recall that the level curves for the function $f(x,y)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=-1.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =c \\ xy-2 & =-1 \\ xy & =1 \\ y & =\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level curve that passes through $P(1,1)$ is the hyperbola $y=\frac{1}{x}.$

contexts.title: Rewriting a Double Integral Over a Circle or Part-Circle Centered at the Origin

canonical.:question/problem:
![](images/17/1782385c55493892be0308ede1e4fbe5308ea9440e21b70cc2da7d7f01fb8dcd.png)

The region $D$ is the quarter-circle shown above. What is $$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_D y \sqrt{x^2+y^2} \: \textrm{d}A
$$
expressed in polar coordinates?
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

First, notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $1$ centered at the origin. In polar coordinates $(r, \theta),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \Big\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 1, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2} \Big\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

contexts.title: Rewriting a Double Integral Over a Circle or Part-Circle Not Centered at the Origin

canonical.:question/problem:
Given that $D = \left\{ (x,y) \, : \, x^2 + (y+2)^2 \leq 4\right\},$ express the following integral in polar coordinates:

$$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_D e^{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}} \, \textrm{d}A
$$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form
$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

First, let's sketch our region $D{:}$

![](images/e4/e447e688e0f3e2c0411129e8d1baf4a900008173443f5392d98af52a27eb285b.png)

Notice that the region $D$ represents the disk of radius $2$ centered at $(0,-2).$ 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:
$$
\left\{  \begin{array}{l}x = r \cos   \theta  \\ y = r \sin   \theta \end{array} \right.
$$

With that in mind, let's now write the $x^2 + (y+2)^2 = 4$ in polar coordinates:
$$
\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle {x}^{2} + ( y + 2 {)}^{2} & \displaystyle  = 4 \\ \displaystyle {( r \cos   \theta  )}^{2} + {( r \sin   \theta  + 2 )}^{2} & \displaystyle  = 4 \\ \displaystyle {r}^{2} {\cos }^{2}  \theta  + {r}^{2} {\sin }^{2}  \theta  + 4 r \sin   \theta  + 4 & \displaystyle  = 4 \\ \displaystyle {r}^{2} ( {\cos }^{2}  \theta  + {\sin }^{2}  \theta  ) + 4 r \sin   \theta  & \displaystyle  = 0 \\ \displaystyle {r}^{2} + 4 r \sin   \theta  & \displaystyle  = 0 \\ \displaystyle r ( r + 4 \sin   \theta  ) & \displaystyle  = 0\end{array}
$$ 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire circle, we must have $r = -4\sin{\theta}.$

Now, let's determine the limits for $r$ and $\theta.$ First of all, $r$ can vary from $r=0$ (at the origin) to $r = -4\sin{\theta}$ (at the boundary of the region): 

![](images/52/522df0e95e36cd67f34ffcc0ec4757c35749eab5d5137215c456c8b7e90994ae.png)

Secondly, $\theta$ can vary between $\theta = \pi$ (the negative $x$-axis) and $\theta  = 2 \pi $ (the positive $x$-axis):

![](images/6a/6ad24b638877941296df25869f8b0ee6f9dc1e73a779a8a0da01de35d9f74f42.png)

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta) \, : \, 0 \leq r \leq -4\sin{\theta}, \, \pi \leq \theta \leq 2\pi \right\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 
$$
\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle \underset{D}{\iint } {e}^{\sqrt{ {x}^{2} + {y}^{2}}} \hspace{0.167em} \text{d} A & \displaystyle  = \underset{\mathrm{\Delta }}{\iint } {e}^{\sqrt{( r \cos   \theta  {)}^{2} + ( r \sin   \theta  {)}^{2}}} \hspace{0.167em} r \hspace{0.167em} \text{d} r \hspace{0.167em} \text{d} \theta  \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\int }_{\pi }^{2 \pi } {\int }_{0}^{- 4 \sin   \theta } r {e}^{\sqrt{ {r}^{2} ( {\cos }^{2}  \theta  + {\sin }^{2}  \theta  )}} \hspace{0.167em} \text{d} r \hspace{0.167em} \text{d} \theta  \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\int }_{\pi }^{2 \pi } {\int }_{0}^{- 4 \sin   \theta } r {e}^{\sqrt{ {r}^{2}}} \hspace{0.167em} \text{d} r \hspace{0.167em} \text{d} \theta  \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\int }_{\pi }^{2 \pi } {\int }_{0}^{- 4 \sin   \theta } r {e}^{r} \hspace{0.167em} \text{d} r \hspace{0.167em} \text{d} \theta  .\end{array}
$$

contexts.title: Evaluating a Triple Integral by Converting to Cylindrical Coordinates

canonical.:question/problem:
Evaluate the triple integral 

$$
\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R x+2y \:\textrm{d}V
$$

over the region $R$ enclosed inside the cylinder $x^2+y^2=5$ for $x\geq 0,$ $y\geq 0$ and between the surfaces $z=y$ and $z=y+3.$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
\iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, \mathrm{d}V = 
\iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta, z) \:  r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta.
$$

If $(r, \theta, z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x = r\cos\theta, \qquad
y = r\sin\theta, \qquad 
z = z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](images/b7/b7b37ffe8e97ed4a661ee98750894641c6ed3354864dd5b54d2ed076e4fdb69b.png)

The region $R$ is a right vertical cylinder of radius $\sqrt{5}$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

- bounded below by $z=y=r\sin\theta,$ and

- bounded above by $z=y+3=r\sin\theta + 3.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta,z) \, : \, 0 \leq r \leq \sqrt{5}, \: 0 \leq \theta \lt \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \: r\sin\theta \leq z \leq r\sin\theta + 3\right\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}x+2y\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{5}}{\int }_{r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }^{r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +3}{r}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{5}}{r}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )[z]_{z=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }^{z=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{5}}{r}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +3-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{5}}3{r}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[{r}^{3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )]_{r=0}^{r=\sqrt{5}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{(\sqrt{5})}^{3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}5\sqrt{5}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =5\sqrt{5}[\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]_{\theta =0}^{\theta =\pi /2} \\  & =5\sqrt{5}(1-0)-10\sqrt{5}(0-1) \\  & =15\sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}x\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}{\int }_{r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }^{r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4}{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta [z]_{z=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }^{z=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta (r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}4{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}[{r}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]_{r=0}^{r=\sqrt{3}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(\sqrt{3})^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}9\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =[9\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ]_{\theta =-\pi /2}^{\theta =\pi /2} \\  & =9(1-(-1)) \\  & =18.\end{aligned}
$$

nearby_complete.:question/problem:
Evaluate the triple integral 

$$
{∭}_{R}\frac{z}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}V
$$

over the region $R$ enclosed inside the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$ and between the surfaces $z=0$ and $z=\sqrt{9-({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})}.$
nearby_complete.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,z)\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta .
$$

If $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z=z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](images/9c/9c4ea0ba92e19a201e3944defa6deb0bc1ee76971adaa809521722b6ac31241f.png)

The region $R$ is a right vertical cylinder of radius $3$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

- bounded below by $z=0,$ and

- bounded above by $$
\displaystyle z=\sqrt{9-({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})}=\sqrt{9-{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}=\sqrt{9-{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}.
$$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta ,z)\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,0\le \theta <2\pi ,\,0\le z\le \sqrt{9-{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\frac{z}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\frac{z}{\sqrt{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }}\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{9-{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}}z\,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}{[\frac{1}{2}{z}^{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=\sqrt{9-{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{2}{(\sqrt{9-{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )})}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{2}(9-{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{[\frac{9}{2}r-\frac{1}{6}{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )]}_{r=0}^{r=3}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{9}{2}(3)-\frac{1}{6}(3)^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{27}{2}-\frac{9}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={[\frac{27}{2}\theta -\frac{9}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )]}_{\theta =0}^{\theta =2\pi } \\  & =\frac{27}{2}(2\pi -0)-\frac{9}{4}(0-0) \\  & =27\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

contexts.title: Rewriting a Double Integral Over a Circle or Part-Circle Not Centered at the Origin

canonical.:question/problem:
Given that $D = \left\{ (x,y) \, : \, x^2 + (y+2)^2 \leq 4\right\},$ express the following integral in polar coordinates:

$$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_D e^{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}} \, \textrm{d}A
$$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form
$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

First, let's sketch our region $D{:}$

![](images/e4/e447e688e0f3e2c0411129e8d1baf4a900008173443f5392d98af52a27eb285b.png)

Notice that the region $D$ represents the disk of radius $2$ centered at $(0,-2).$ 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:
$$
\left\{  \begin{array}{l}x = r \cos   \theta  \\ y = r \sin   \theta \end{array} \right.
$$

With that in mind, let's now write the $x^2 + (y+2)^2 = 4$ in polar coordinates:
$$
\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle {x}^{2} + ( y + 2 {)}^{2} & \displaystyle  = 4 \\ \displaystyle {( r \cos   \theta  )}^{2} + {( r \sin   \theta  + 2 )}^{2} & \displaystyle  = 4 \\ \displaystyle {r}^{2} {\cos }^{2}  \theta  + {r}^{2} {\sin }^{2}  \theta  + 4 r \sin   \theta  + 4 & \displaystyle  = 4 \\ \displaystyle {r}^{2} ( {\cos }^{2}  \theta  + {\sin }^{2}  \theta  ) + 4 r \sin   \theta  & \displaystyle  = 0 \\ \displaystyle {r}^{2} + 4 r \sin   \theta  & \displaystyle  = 0 \\ \displaystyle r ( r + 4 \sin   \theta  ) & \displaystyle  = 0\end{array}
$$ 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire circle, we must have $r = -4\sin{\theta}.$

Now, let's determine the limits for $r$ and $\theta.$ First of all, $r$ can vary from $r=0$ (at the origin) to $r = -4\sin{\theta}$ (at the boundary of the region): 

![](images/52/522df0e95e36cd67f34ffcc0ec4757c35749eab5d5137215c456c8b7e90994ae.png)

Secondly, $\theta$ can vary between $\theta = \pi$ (the negative $x$-axis) and $\theta  = 2 \pi $ (the positive $x$-axis):

![](images/6a/6ad24b638877941296df25869f8b0ee6f9dc1e73a779a8a0da01de35d9f74f42.png)

So, in polar coordinates $(r, \theta),$ the region can be expressed as 
$$
\Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta) \, : \, 0 \leq r \leq -4\sin{\theta}, \, \pi \leq \theta \leq 2\pi \right\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 
$$
\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle \underset{D}{\iint } {e}^{\sqrt{ {x}^{2} + {y}^{2}}} \hspace{0.167em} \text{d} A & \displaystyle  = \underset{\mathrm{\Delta }}{\iint } {e}^{\sqrt{( r \cos   \theta  {)}^{2} + ( r \sin   \theta  {)}^{2}}} \hspace{0.167em} r \hspace{0.167em} \text{d} r \hspace{0.167em} \text{d} \theta  \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\int }_{\pi }^{2 \pi } {\int }_{0}^{- 4 \sin   \theta } r {e}^{\sqrt{ {r}^{2} ( {\cos }^{2}  \theta  + {\sin }^{2}  \theta  )}} \hspace{0.167em} \text{d} r \hspace{0.167em} \text{d} \theta  \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\int }_{\pi }^{2 \pi } {\int }_{0}^{- 4 \sin   \theta } r {e}^{\sqrt{ {r}^{2}}} \hspace{0.167em} \text{d} r \hspace{0.167em} \text{d} \theta  \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\int }_{\pi }^{2 \pi } {\int }_{0}^{- 4 \sin   \theta } r {e}^{r} \hspace{0.167em} \text{d} r \hspace{0.167em} \text{d} \theta  .\end{array}
$$

contexts.title: Evaluating Repeated Integrals Expressed in Polar Coordinates

canonical.:question/problem:
Evaluate $$
\displaystyle \int_{0}^{\pi/8} \int_0^{\sin2\theta} r \, \textrm d r\,\textrm d \theta.
$$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
First, we integrate with respect to $r,$ treating $\theta$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}{[{r}^{2}]}_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}{sin}^{2}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the double-angle formula

$$
\cos{2x} = 1-2\sin^2 x.
$$

Substituting $x=2\theta$ and rearranging, we get

$$
\sin^22\theta = \dfrac12\left(1-\cos4\theta\right).
$$

 

Finally, we can finish our integral by integrating with respect to $\theta,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}{sin}^{2}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}1-\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{[\theta -\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta ]}_{0}^{\pi /8} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[(\frac{\pi }{8}-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right))-(0-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\frac{\pi }{8}-\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\frac{\pi }{8}-\frac{2}{8}) \\  & =\frac{1}{32}(\pi -2)\end{aligned}
$$

canonical.:question/problem:
The region $R$ is enclosed inside the cylinder $x^2 + y^2 = 4$ for $y \geq 0$ between the surfaces $z =0$ and $z = 10 - x.$ Express the following triple integral in cylindrical polar coordinates. 

$$
\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R y \:\textrm{d}V
$$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
\iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, \mathrm{d}V = 
\iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta, z) \:  r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta.
$$

If $(r, \theta, z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x = r\cos\theta, \qquad
y = r\sin\theta, \qquad 
z = z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](images/9a/9ad0d507a5440cfce9595e9054457fd733ae412d9a57b0a85238b4773ff0a0c7.png)

The region $R$ is one-half of a right vertical cylinder of radius $2$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

- bounded below by $z=0,$ and

- bounded above by $z=10-x = 10 - r\cos\theta.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta,z) \, : \, 0 \leq r \leq 2, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq \pi, \: 0 \leq z \leq 10-r\cos\theta \right\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}y\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\cdot r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{10-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

canonical.:question/problem: Sketch the graph of $y=-\dfrac{1}{2}x+3.$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
We need to find two distinct points that lie on our line. Any two points will do!

It is often easiest to pick one of the points to have an $x$-coordinate of $x=0.$ So, for the first point, we will let the $x$-coordinate be $x=0.$ Then the $y$-coordinate is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{1}{2}x+3 \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(0)+3 \\  & =0+3 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the first point is $(0,3).$

For the second point, let's choose $x=4.$ Then the $y$-coordinate is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{1}{2}x+3 \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(4)+3 \\  & =-2+3 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second point is $(4,1).$

Finally, we plot those two points on the $xy$-plane and draw a line through them. This is the graph of $y=-\dfrac{1}{2}x+3.$

![](images/36/36689081acaacb24a09826c3927388697e77d92caeca900d053d33d0f99d2b8c.png)

contexts.title: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Curve Defined Parametrically

canonical.:question/problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the curve defined parametrically by

$$
x=2t^2, \,\,\, y=t^2+1, \quad t \geq 0.
$$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
To find the Cartesian equation, we eliminate $t.$ First we use the $x$ equation to solve for $t^2\mathbin{:}$

$$
x=2t^2 \quad \Rightarrow\quad  t^2 = \dfrac{x}{2}
$$

Now substituting $t^2=\dfrac{x}{2}$ into our expression for $y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={t}^{2}+1 \\  & =\frac{x}{2}+1 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is $y=\dfrac{1}{2}x+1.$

Finally, since $t \geq0$ and $x=2t^2,$ we must have $x \geq 0.$

So, the complete Cartesian equation is

$$
y=\dfrac{1}{2}x+1, \quad x \geq 0 .
$$

nearby_complete.:question/problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the curve defined parametrically by

$$
x=\frac{1}{t-2},\,\,\,y={t}^{2},\,t\ne 2.
$$
nearby_complete.:question/worked-solution:
To find the Cartesian equation, we eliminate $t.$ First, we use the $x$ equation to solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{1}{t-2} \\ x(t-2) & =1 \\ t-2 & =\frac{1}{x} \\ t & =\frac{1}{x}+2 \\ t & =\frac{1+2x}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now substituting $t=\frac{1+2x}{x}$ into our expression for $y={t}^{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={\left(\frac{1+2x}{x}\right)}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is $y={\left(\frac{1+2x}{x}\right)}^{2}.$

Finally, since $t\ne 2$ and $x=\frac{1}{t-2},$ we must have $x\ne 0.$

So, the complete Cartesian equation is

$$
y={\left(\frac{1+2x}{x}\right)}^{2},\,x\ne 0.
$$

nearby_complete.:question/problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the curve defined parametrically by

$$
x=1-2t,\,\,\,y=(t-2)^{2}(t+1),\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$
nearby_complete.:question/worked-solution:
To find the Cartesian equation, we eliminate $t.$ First, we use the $x$ equation to solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x=1-2t\,⇒\,t=\frac{1-x}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $t=\frac{1-x}{2}$ into our expression for $y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={(\frac{1-x}{2}-2)}^{2}(\frac{1-x}{2}+1) \\  & ={\left(\frac{1-x-4}{2}\right)}^{2}\left(\frac{1-x+2}{2}\right) \\  & ={\left(\frac{-x-3}{2}\right)}^{2}\left(\frac{3-x}{2}\right) \\  & =-\frac{1}{8}(x+3)^{2}(x-3).\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is $y=-\frac{1}{8}(x+3)^{2}(x-3).$

nearby_complete.:question/problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the curve defined parametrically by

$$
x=\frac{t-5}{2},\,\,\,y=({t}^{2}-25)(t-4),\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$
nearby_complete.:question/worked-solution:
To find the Cartesian equation, we eliminate $t.$ First, we use the $x$ equation to solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\frac{t-5}{2}\,⇒\,t=2x+5\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $t=2x+5$ into our expression for $y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =((2x+5)^{2}-25)(2x+5-4) \\  & =(4{x}^{2}+20x+25-25)(2x+1) \\  & =(4{x}^{2}+20x)(2x+1) \\  & =4x(x+5)(2x+1).\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is $y=4x(x+5)(2x+1).$

canonical.:question/problem: Let $\mathbf{a}=\langle 4,2,-1 \rangle,$ $\mathbf{b}=\langle 0,2,1 \rangle,$ and $\mathbf{c}=\langle -1,-1,2 \rangle.$ Find $\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}).$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that the scalar triple product $\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c})$ is just the determinant of the matrix whose rows are given by $\mathbf{a},$ $\mathbf{b},$ and $\mathbf{c}.$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot (b\times c) & =\begin{vmatrix}4 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =4\cdot \begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{vmatrix}-2\cdot \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{vmatrix}+(-1)\cdot \begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ -1 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =4\cdot (2\cdot 2-1\cdot (-1))-2\cdot (0\cdot 2-1\cdot (-1))+(-1)\cdot (0\cdot (-1)-2\cdot (-1)) \\  & =20-2-2 \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

contexts.title: Finding an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Curve

canonical.:question/problem:
Write down the integral that gives the arc length of the curve  $\mathbf f (t) = \langle 3 \sin t, \: 2\sin 2t \rangle$
from $t =\dfrac {3\pi} 2$  to $t = 2\pi.$

![](images/57/574a16e843a9c81e5fc9ddbbe2c0dc2c308ffcac4991bcbf48c7f45b4871c93b.png)
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find $\mathbf f'(t)$ and $\|\mathbf f'(t)\|\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩ \\ ‖{f}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(4\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9{cos}^{2}⁡t+16{cos}^{2}⁡2t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{a}^{b}‖{f}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }\sqrt{9{cos}^{2}⁡t+16{cos}^{2}⁡2t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

contexts.title: Computing the Arc Length of a Three-Dimensional Spatial Curve

canonical.:question/problem:
![](images/85/8573aedcd26cba038b2db072560cd3d6ba7676542888a2d9b8a356713eaf6724.png)

Find the arc length of the curve $\mathbf r (t) = \langle \sin t ,\: \cos t, \: t \rangle$
from  $t =0$ to $t = 2\pi.$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find $\mathbf r'(t)$ and $\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t+1} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\text{ }\sqrt{2}\,t{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\sqrt{2}(2\pi -0) \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

contexts.title: Finding the Equation of a Level Curve

canonical.:question/problem: Find the equation of the level curve that passes through the point $G\big(\sqrt{5}, 1\big)$ for the function $f(x,y) = \dfrac{12y}{x^2-y^2}.$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the value of the function at $G$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
  f\big(\sqrt{5}, 1\big)&= \dfrac{12(1)}{\big(\sqrt{5}\big)^2 - 1^2} = 3\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the level curve that passes through $G\big(\sqrt{5}, 1\big)$ is the $3$-level curve.

Recall that the level curves for the function $f(x,y)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y) = c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=3.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =c \\ \frac{12y}{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} & =3 \\ 4y & ={x}^{2}-{y}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-4y-4 & =-4 \\ {x}^{2}-({y}^{2}+4y+4) & =-4 \\ {x}^{2}-(y+2)^{2} & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level curve that passes through $G\big(\sqrt{5}, 1\big)$ is the hyperbola $x^2 - (y+2)^2 = -4.$

$$

Therefore, the level curve that passes through $P(1,1)$ is the hyperbola $y=\frac{1}{x}.$

contexts.title: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Parametrized Circle

canonical.:question/problem:
Calculate the Cartesian equation of the circle

$$
x=3\cos\theta + 2,\quad y=3\sin\theta - 4, \quad 0\leq\theta\lt 2\pi.
$$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta.$ We can do this using the Pythagorean identity:

$$
\cos^2 \theta + \sin^2 \theta = 1
$$

By isolating the $\cos\theta$ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-2}{3} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{{3}^{2}} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{9} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\sin\theta$ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y+4}{3} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(y+4)^{2}}{{3}^{2}} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(y+4)^{2}}{9} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these values into the Pythagorean identity, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{9}+\frac{(y+4)^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ (x-2)^{2}+(y+4)^{2} & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation is $(x-2)^2 + (y+4)^2 = 9.$

By isolating the $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(y+\frac{1}{2}) & =5\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{1}{5}(y+\frac{1}{2}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{1}{25}{(y+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{25}{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+\frac{1}{25}{(y+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{1}{25}{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+\frac{1}{25}{(y+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =1 \\ {(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{(y+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =25.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation is $$
\displaystyle {(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{(y+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}=25.
$$

contexts.title: Determining the Range of a Parametric Equation

canonical.:question/problem:
Given that a curve is defined parametrically as

$$
x=t^2-6t, \,\,\, y=t^4+4, \quad t \in (-\infty , \infty),
$$

what are the ranges of $x$ and $y?$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
Let's consider each variable in turn.

- To find the range of $x,$ we can start by completing the square, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={t}^{2}-6t \\  & ={(t-3)}^{2}-(3)^{2} \\  & ={(t-3)}^{2}-9\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\left( t-3\right)^2 \geq 0,$ we can conclude that $x \geq -9.$

- To find the range of $y=t^4+4,$ notice that $t^4 \geq 0,$ and consequently $y \geq 4.$

Therefore, the ranges are $x \geq -9$ and $y \geq 4.$

$$

Since ${(t+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}\ge 0,$ we can conclude that $x\ge -\frac{1}{4}.$

- To find the range of $y,$ notice that ${t}^{2}\ge 0.$ Therefore, we can conclude that $y\ge -2.$

So, the ranges are $x\ge -\frac{1}{4}$ and $y\ge -2.$

contexts.title: Determining the Range of a Parametric Equation Defined in Terms of Trigonometric Functions

canonical.:question/problem:
Given that a curve is defined parametrically as

$$
x = 4\cos\theta, \,\,\, y = 2\sin\theta, \quad 0\leq \theta <     2\pi,
$$

what are the ranges of $x$ and $y?$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
Let's consider each variable in turn.

- To find the range of $x,$ notice that for $0\leq\theta <  2\pi,$ we have $-1 \leq \cos{\theta} \leq 1.$ Consequently,

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & \le \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \le 1 \\ -4 & \le 4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \le 4 \\ -4 & \le x\le 4.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can conclude that $-4 \leq x \leq 4.$

- To find the range of $y,$ notice that for $0\leq\theta <  2\pi,$ we have $-1 \leq \sin{\theta} \leq 1.$ Consequently,

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & \le \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \le 1 \\ -2 & \le 2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \le 2 \\ -2 & \le y\le 2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can conclude that $-2 \leq y \leq 2.$

Therefore, the ranges are $-4 \leq x \leq 4$ and $-2 \leq y \leq 2.$

x=7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=7\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

What is the domain of the parameter $\theta ?$
nearby_complete.:question/worked-solution:
The parametric equations of a circle  of radius $r$  centered at  the origin are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

In our case, the radius $r=7.$ So, the parametric equations of the *full* circle are 

$$
x=7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=7\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

To restrict the parameterization to a semi-circle, we associate the parameter $\theta $ with the central angle formed by a point $(x,y)$ on the circle and the $x$-axis. 

![](images/25/25503e83f9a196cab4ded2fd93b09028b1608bd7d815edd538564e1aa611ca86.png)

We can see that if we restrict $\theta $ to $[0,\pi ]$, we get the required semi-circle.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the semi-circle are 

$$
x=7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=7\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,\pi ].
$$
